tagline: An old lakeside road follows Superior past cliffs and waterfalls.
intro: The North Shore Scenic Drive follows Lake Superior from Duluth to the Canadian border, between the rocky shore and the foothills of the Sawtooth Range. Along the highway, the shoreline journey includes forests and cliffs, with the lake lying to the southeast. The Federal Highway Administration lists this 154-mile route as an All-American Road, highlighting access to eight state parks and the Superior National Forest. It suggests three hours for the drive, or one to two days with stops.

Road access came in stages: the Duluth-to-border highway became part of U.S. 61 in 1926, was ready for use by 1929 and was paved by 1940. In the 1960s, an inland expressway replaced the original stretch between Duluth and Two Harbors. The old road passed to the counties as Scenic 61; north of Duluth, the U.S. highway designation became Minnesota 61 in 1991.

Leaving Duluth, the byway uses County 61 toward Two Harbors, then follows Minnesota 61 northeast. Beyond Two Harbors the highway narrows to two lanes, passing Gooseberry Falls and Split Rock Lighthouse State Park before Beaver Bay and Silver Bay. Continue through Lutsen and Grand Marais toward Grand Portage, which the highway bypasses to the west, before reaching the Pigeon River border crossing.

moments.title: Gooseberry Falls State Park
moments.text: Three layers of lava are visible from the highway bridge at Gooseberry Falls. The river has cut through the flows, descending from the uppermost layer toward Lake Superior; the park includes Upper, Middle and Lower Falls. Preservation began with legislative authorization in 1933; state park designation followed in 1937, during the construction program. Stone also defines the park buildings: Civilian Conservation Corps crews built its rustic structures between 1934 and 1941, using red, blue, brown and black basalt. The National Park Service’s Minnesota Central Design Office supervised the designs, while two Italian stonemasons supervised construction.
moments.notice: From the highway bridge, look for three distinct lava layers.

moments.title: Split Rock Lighthouse
moments.text: Split Rock’s octagonal tower stands on a 133-foot cliff above Lake Superior. The United States Lighthouse Service completed it in 1910 after the ship losses of the 1905 Mataafa Storm. With no roads to the site, builders brought materials by water and lifted them up the cliff by crane. The Coast Guard retired the light in 1969. The Minnesota Historical Society operates the site, which retains the original tower and lens, along with the fog signal building and keepers’ houses. Each November 10, the light shines in memory of the Edmund Fitzgerald, which sank on that date in 1975.
moments.notice: The octagonal brick tower rises from a cliff 133 feet high.

moments.title: Grand Portage National Monument
moments.text: An 8.5-mile footpath bypasses the waterfalls and rapids on the Pigeon River’s last 20 miles. Voyageurs carried fur bundles from Fort Charlotte to Grand Portage, where they exchanged them with Montreal traders for goods and supplies. The depot here is reconstructed. The Heritage Center, opened in 2007 through collaboration between the National Park Service and the Grand Portage Band of Lake Superior Chippewa, overlooks it. Its galleries interpret Ojibwe culture and the fur trade. The Great Hall’s corner rooms follow the trade from furs and exchange goods to finished products and a hatter’s workshop.
